title: High spectral resolution second harmonic generation microspectroscopy at thin layer interfaces with broadband continuum pulses
author: Mokim, Card, et al.

steps.title: Generate broadband femtosecond continuum
steps.instruction: Produce spectrally tailored near‑infrared femtosecond continuum pulses with a smooth envelope spanning >350 nm, centered between 780 nm and 1050 nm, by launching a high‑repetition‑rate laser into a photonic‑crystal fiber (PCF) that provides superior spatial quality and stable spectral power density.

steps.title: Prepare TMDC and reference samples
steps.instruction: Place the atomically thin TMDC monolayer (e.g., WSe₂ or WS₂) on a 90 nm SiO₂ layer on a thick Si substrate, and position a bulk KTP crystal (χ_B(2)=1.98 pm V⁻¹) as the reference material in the same optical path.

steps.title: Focus beam onto samples
steps.instruction: Using an objective lens with known numerical aperture Θ, focus the continuum beam onto the TMDC sample and, simultaneously, onto the KTP crystal so that second‑harmonic generation (SHG) is collected in the backward direction from each.

steps.title: Record SHG spectra
steps.instruction: With a spectrometer capable of ≤2 meV (≈0.3 nm at 450 nm) resolution and <5–6 % rms noise, acquire the SHG spectrum from the TMDC (photon‑energy range 2.4–3.2 eV) and from the KTP reference under identical illumination conditions.

steps.title: Normalize SHG signal
steps.instruction: Compute the ratio ρ_ω = S_2D / S_B where S_2D is the SHG intensity from the TMDC and S_B is the SHG intensity from the KTP crystal at each photon energy; apply the ξ_ω‑factor correction (as defined in Ref. [6]) to obtain the corrected ratio.

steps.title: Calculate absolute χ₂D
steps.instruction: Insert the corrected ratio into the formula χ_2D² = 32πc Θ² n_B + (1/3) n_B ω ρ_ω ξ_ω χ_B(2) (where n_B is the effective refractive index of KTP, ω the fundamental angular frequency, and c the speed of light) to obtain the absolute second‑order susceptibility χ_2D(2) of the monolayer.

steps.title: Analyze dispersion and extract parameters
steps.instruction: Plot χ_2D(2) versus SH photon energy (2.4–3.2 eV). Identify the main peak (maximum ≈0.78 × 10⁻¹⁸ m² V⁻¹ at 2.79 eV, width ≈250 meV) and any sub‑structure (e.g., features ~250 meV apart). From the peak positions infer exciton‑related transitions (e.g., B‑exciton near Eg + Δ_so ≈2.5–2.9 eV). For WS₂, repeat the procedure to obtain its bandgap (≈2.38 ± 0.06 eV) and exciton binding energy (≈0.36 ± 0.06 eV).

description: Atomically thin layers of transitional metal dichalcogenides (TMDC) have attracted very strong interest due to their unique semiconducting and transport properties that give a strong promise for their practical applications. Important physical properties and parameters of these 2D semiconductors, such as bandstructure in quasi-momentum space, fundamental bandgap, dispersion of dielectric function, exciton effects and enhanced optical nonlinearities, are currently the focus of the comprehensive research. Linear and nonlinear response in the optical frequency range is a prime source of information that can answer the fundamental questions. Several groups have recently reported second harmonic generation (SHG) studies of monolayer TMDCs [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]]. The most comprehensive study was performed by Wang et al. [5] at low temperatures with the experiments focused on obtaining second order nonlinearity (χ(2)) dispersion at the near bandgap photon energies (1.75–2.35 eV). The experiments were performed with a picosecond pulse source that was wavelength tuned point-by-point and used as the fundamental frequency beam. While the results make sense, significant measurement errors in the study impact the data due to variations in temporal, spectral and spatial properties of the fundamental beam at different wavelengths. Fig. 4 shows spectral data for SHG obtained from WSe2 single layer (blue curve) and bulk KTP crystal (green curve) when the broadband continuum beam was incident on the two nonlinear media. One can see that the shapes of the two curves are drastically different. The effective length of the nonlinear interaction within the KTP crystal is about 0.7 μm. Nevertheless, the SHG signal from single layer (zero thickness) WSe2 is about two times higher at around 450 nm (˜2.75 eV).
